newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian prince says undeterred by Hun Sen threat.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian prince says undeterred by Hun Sen threat.

text.p: Cambodia's exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh has dismissed threats by Second Prime Minster Hun Sen to forcibly block his return to Phnom Penh, calling the premier a "terrorist" for vowing to shoot down his plane.

Sirivudh said in a telephone interview from France late on Sunday night that he was still planning to return to Cambodia, and suggested that high officials in his royalist FUNCINPEC party would help protect him.

"Hun Sen is a terrorist because he wants to shoot down my airplane. Ask him, how many people will be on board?" said Sirivudh, referring to Hun Sen's threat on Sunday to hit any plane bringing the prince back from France.
Hun Sen had also said he had tanks and heavy weapons ready in Phnom Penh to stop the return of Sirivudh, who was arrested in November 1995 for allegedly plotting to assassinate Hun Sen.

Sirivudh is the half-brother of King Norodom Sihanouk. He agreed to go into exile in France rather than go to court, but was sentenced in absentia to 10 years in jail in a trial that international observers branded a travesty.
Sirivudh said he had set no date for his return, but that he would not change his plans to come home.

"I thank (deputy chief of staff Lieutenant General) Nhiek Bun Chhay and (First Prime Minister) Prince Norodom Ranariddh very much for supporting me and saying they would protect me when I return," he said.

Ranariddh, who is serving as a Buddhist monk for one week according to royal family tradition, was unavailable for comment. The prince, who left for a one-day pilgrimage to India on Monday, cannot discuss politics while in the monkhood.
Analysts said the fate of Sirivudh had heightened ire between Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and Hun Sen, who have long been at odds.
The dispute over Sirivudh, which has become a lightning rod in the conflict between the two leaders, will pose the biggest challenge yet for Cambodia's uneasy coalition government, they said.
